query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy that is initially in a non-equilibrium metastable solid solution, moderate thermal exposure triggers a two‐step kinetic transformation: first, the nucleation of nanoscale, grain‐boundary–localized intermetallic precipitates enriched in Mg and passivating elements (e.g., Ti, Zn) fosters the formation of a protective oxide film (such as TiO2 or mixed oxides) that preserves or even enhances corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance; however, with excessive thermal exposure, these intermetallic particles coarsen and interconnect to form continuous networks that disrupt the uniformity of the passivating layer, leading to a marked loss of corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight HEA in a metastable, non-equilibrium solid solution state with a uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging/annealing at service-relevant temperatures.
generation.conditions: Thermal exposure in a regime near the operating temperatures (e.g., ~450–550 °C) and durations varied to capture early-stage nucleation versus advanced coarsening; subsequent tests include salt-spray corrosion and high-temperature oxidation (850–1050 °C) environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The size, distribution, and connectivity of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates (especially Mg-rich and Ti/Zn-enriched phases) that evolve during the thermal treatment.
generation.mechanism: The inherent sluggish diffusion in HEAs controls a two-stage phase transformation. Initially, limited diffusion promotes heterogeneous nucleation of fine intermetallics at grain boundaries that concentrate alloying elements favorable for forming protective oxides. As diffusion continues with prolonged exposure, these precipitates coarsen and eventually form interconnected networks that interrupt the continuity of the passivating oxide scale, thus accelerating both corrosion and oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A controlled thermal treatment leads to a bimodal behavior: (1) short-to-moderate exposures yield a microstructure with finely dispersed intermetallics that sustain or even improve corrosion/oxidation resistance by supporting a stable passivating layer, whereas (2) prolonged exposure results in coarsened, continuous intermetallic networks that degrade the protective oxide film, observable as increased corrosion current densities and faster oxidation kinetics relative to the initial state.
generation.baseline: The as-processed metastable solid solution state that exhibits superior corrosion and oxidation resistance due to its uniform elemental distribution and absence of significant intermetallic coarsening.
generation.boundary: Service conditions are limited to temperatures and durations that maintain fine-scale intermetallic dispersion (e.g., below the threshold where intermetallic coarsening becomes continuous, likely under 600 °C and for shorter exposure times); beyond these, the protective properties deteriorate.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends the kinetic phase-tailoring insights from PMC5043342 (which demonstrated that cooling and annealing rates control phase selection in HEAs) and the corrosion/passivation observations from PMC12299034 (which linked the distribution of fine intermetallics to enhanced passivation in Mg-Ti-Zn alloys). The new aspect is applying a two-stage kinetic framework to predict when beneficial fine precipitates transition into deleterious coarsened networks in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs. Uncertainty remains regarding the precise thresholds (in time and temperature) and the role of competing diffusion rates among Mg and other alloying elements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare billets of the target Mg-containing lightweight HEA in the metastable solid-solution state. Divide the samples into groups and subject them to controlled thermal exposures at, for example, 500 °C, for varying durations (short, moderate, prolonged). After each treatment, characterize the microstructure via TEM and SEM-EDS to determine the size, distribution, and connectivity of intermetallic precipitates. Then, perform corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization in NaCl solution) and high-temperature oxidation tests (using thermogravimetric analysis in an oxygen-rich atmosphere). A side-by-side controlled comparison with the as-cast, unaged material should be maintained.
measurements: Microstructural imaging (TEM, SEM, possibly atom probe tomography) to evaluate intermetallic particle size and distribution.
Thermogravimetric analysis for oxidation kinetics (mass gain vs time at 850–1050 °C).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if no statistically significant correlation is observed between the extent of intermetallic coarsening (i.e., transition from fine, dispersed particles to interconnected networks) and a corresponding degradation in corrosion and oxidation resistance. In other words, if samples with coarsened intermetallic structures display the same or improved protective oxide characteristics and similar corrosion current densities as the initial metastable state, the proposed mechanistic pathway would be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: The MgTiZn (TZ) and Mg4TiZn (4TZ) alloys developed in this study demonstrated a rare combination of high hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance, which are often mutually exclusive in Mg-based systems. As illustrated in the schematic cross-sections (Figure 9), the TZ alloy exhibited a microstructure containing abundant intermetallic phases (Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25) within a Ti- and Zn-enriched matrix (confirmed by the STEM analysis) and fine oxide particles (TiOx and MgO). In contrast, 4TZ presented a more homogeneous Mg-rich matrix containing solid solution domains composed of Mg, Ti, and Zn, and larger Ti rich regions. The presence of Ti and Zn in the matrix, along with uniformly distributed fine intermetallics, promoted the formation of a protective surface film (observed via XPS), leading to passivation and high corrosion resistance. Although micropores were observed in both alloys (Figure 1), which are typically expected to increase corrosion susceptibility, the corrosion current densities of the alloys remained low, suggesting that the protective effect of passivating surface films and refined microstructures outweighed the detrimental influence of porosity. cited_evidence.text: Our results indicated that kinetics of phase transformation plays a crucial role in phase selection of the CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA. The phases can be controlled using kinetic ways according to the CCT curve. It seems that the sluggish diffusion in HEAs did not affect the kinetic behavior in this alloy system especially in the intermediate temperature. In fact, kinetic effect not only works for the special CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA but affects the phase selection of all HEAs. Li et al. reported that BCC phase can be obtained by supercooling method in the well-known FCC single phase CoCrFeNi HEA and the mechanical properties of the HEA was enhanced by three times. The rapid solidification behavior of CoCrCuNiFex HEA was also studied and useful nano-phases were found in the matrix, which would unquestionably strengthen the HEA dramatically. Ravi et al. reported that synthesis route can have a significant influence on the process of phase-choice and -evolution in different HEAs and this is actually a result of kinetic effect.
